Hello, my name is Asima and my friend is Aliya. 

We both love astrophysics and very eager to participate in this challenge. 

By taking part in this hackaton we would like to get more experience and broaden our network of Astrophysics enthusiasts.
summary: Comets, asteroids, stars, brown dwarfs, and even new planets reveal themselves by shifting position between images, but no one person can sift through all that data alone. Your challenge is to create a public-facing web tool to display images of the sky from SPHERE mission, making it easy for anyone to quickly see how they change over time.
details:
Platen

Platen is a free web tool for blinking SPHEREx images, the way astronomers once blinked photographic plates. You enter coordinates or pick a preset target. Platen then pulls every SPHEREx image of that spot from NASA/IPAC IRSA, lines them up north-up and plays them as a short movie, one frame per six-month sky survey. Anything that moves or changes brightness, like a brown dwarf, an asteroid or a variable star, shows up as you watch.

Key features

  • Blink, minus-median (moving objects show up as black-and-white pairs), A−B difference and stacking
  • Coadded, single-array or false-colour views, where cold brown dwarfs glow red
  • Tap any source to get its spectrum (0.75–5 µm) or a light curve
  • Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 markers shifted to each epoch, plus an Aladin Lite panel
  • Adjustable field of view, contamination flags, shareable links and embed code
  • A candidate list you can export to report finds

Impact
SPHEREx will image over a billion objects. That's too many for professional astronomers to check by eye. Volunteers have already found most known brown dwarfs by comparing images, and Platen lets anyone do the same in a browser on any device. It also works in class for teaching proper motion, parallax and infrared spectra.

How it's built
Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with our own FITS reader and WCS code (including SIP distortion). A small Python server caches archive requests. The data comes from IRSA (SPHEREx SIA2 and cutouts), CDS VizieR and Aladin Lite. It's hosted on GitHub Pages and Render.

Creativity
The name comes from the glass plates Clyde Tombaugh blinked to find Pluto. We use SPHEREx's 102 bands as a colour cue for discovery. A cold Y dwarf like WISE 0855 can't be seen below 3 µm but is bright at 4.5 µm. Catalog markers move with their stars, so a source with no Gaia match stands out right away. Preset targets are moved from J2000 to their positions today.

What we considered
We wanted it to load a target in one tap, including on phones. Server-side cutouts keep downloads small. Because the archive is queried live, new data releases show up on their own. Bad pixels are masked and contamination flags stay visible. If the archive can't be reached, Platen switches to a simulation, clearly labelled, so demos and lessons still work. Everything is open source and uses only public data.
